title: Power, Performance & Scaling
summary: Why clock speeds stopped climbing around 4 GHz, and how power — not transistors — became the wall CPU design bangs against.

blocks.markdown:
For decades, faster CPU meant higher clock speed. That stopped around 2005 — not because we ran out of transistors, but because we ran out of **power budget**.

- Every switching transistor burns power and dumps it as **heat**.
- Past a point, a chip can't shed heat fast enough to run hotter.
- That single limit reshaped CPU design: multicore, DVFS, dark silicon.

Power isn't just a battery number — it's a design constraint.

- **Heat:** power in becomes heat out; unremoved heat raises temperature until the chip throttles or fails.
- **Battery:** on phones and laptops, power drawn directly limits runtime.
- **Cost:** cooling, power delivery, and electricity all scale with watts used, even in a data center.

Every extra watt has to go somewhere — that "somewhere" is the real limit.

blocks.subTitle: Dynamic power
blocks.markdown:
**Dynamic power** is burned when transistors actually switch on/off.

- Roughly **P ∝ C · V² · f** — capacitance, voltage squared, clock frequency.
- Voltage has the biggest effect since it's squared: halve it, quarter the power.
- Raise the clock (**f**) to go faster, and power rises right along with it.

This is the term chip designers fight hardest to shrink.

blocks.subTitle: Static (leakage) power
blocks.markdown:
**Static power** (leakage) is burned even when a transistor is switched "off" — current still trickles through it.

- Shrinking transistors makes their insulating layers thinner, so more current leaks.
- Unlike dynamic power, leakage doesn't need clock activity — it drains power just from being powered on.
- At today's tiny transistor sizes, leakage is a major share of total power, not a rounding error.

blocks.subTitle: Moore vs Dennard
blocks.markdown:
Two separate predictions get confused constantly.

| | Moore's law | Dennard scaling |
|---|---|---|
| Says | Transistor count doubles every ~2 years | Power density stays constant as transistors shrink |
| Status today | Still roughly holding | Broke down around **2005** |

Moore's law gave us more transistors. Dennard scaling was supposed to let us run them faster for free — it didn't last.

blocks.subTitle: Why Dennard scaling ended
blocks.markdown:
**Dennard scaling** assumed voltage could keep shrinking alongside transistor size, keeping power density flat.

- Below a certain size, voltage couldn't drop further without transistors leaking too much and losing their on/off distinction.
- Once voltage stalled, smaller transistors no longer meant lower power per transistor.
- Result: pack more transistors in the same area, and power density starts **climbing** instead of holding steady.

The **power wall** is the point where raising clock speed further would need more cooling than is practical.

<<< Image: simple line chart, blue/grey palette, x-axis '1990–2020', two lines: 'Clock speed (GHz)' rising then flattening hard near 2005 around 4 GHz, and 'Core count' staying flat then rising steadily after 2005. Minimal labels, generous whitespace. >>>

Clock speeds plateaued near **~4 GHz** around 2005 — pushing higher raised heat faster than any affordable cooling could remove it.

With single-core speed capped by the power wall, the industry pivoted to using extra transistors differently.

- Instead of one faster core, chips added **more cores** running at moderate, power-efficient clocks.
- Total throughput can still rise — if the workload can actually be split across cores.
- This is why software had to start caring about parallelism. See [multicore-multiprocessing](multicore-multiprocessing).

blocks.subTitle: DVFS
blocks.markdown:
**DVFS** (dynamic voltage/frequency scaling) lets a chip adjust its own voltage and clock speed on the fly.

- Light workload → drop voltage and frequency, save power.
- Heavy burst → ramp both up, within the thermal budget.
- This is why a phone CPU idles cool but can briefly "boost" for a demanding app.

blocks.subTitle: Race-to-idle
blocks.markdown:
**Race-to-idle** is the opposite instinct to DVFS's "slow down to save power": run at full speed to finish fast, then drop to a low-power idle state.

- Finishing sooner can burn less total energy than crawling along slowly, since idle draws very little power.
- Best for short bursty tasks; DVFS's steady throttling suits sustained loads better.
- Real chips blend both depending on the workload shape.

**Dark silicon** is chip area with transistors on it that can't all be powered at once within the power budget.

- More transistors fit each generation (Moore's law), but power caps how many can run simultaneously — so parts sit idle, or "dark."
- This pushed the industry's yardstick from raw speed to **performance-per-watt**: useful work done per unit of energy.
- Specialized units (GPUs, NPUs) exist partly because a dedicated circuit does more work per watt than a general core.

Common mistakes:

- **"Clock speed stalled because transistors stopped shrinking."** No — Moore's law kept going; it was Dennard scaling (power) that broke.
- **"More cores always means more speed."** Only if the workload parallelizes; serial code gains nothing from extra cores.
- **"DVFS and race-to-idle are the same idea."** One slows down to save power, the other speeds up to finish and rest.

blocks.subTitle: Moore's law vs Dennard scaling
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Moore's law vs Dennard scaling — what's the difference?**

**Moore's law** predicts transistor count doubling roughly every two years — still holding. **Dennard scaling** predicted power density would stay constant as transistors shrank, so smaller meant faster for free. That broke around 2005 once voltage couldn't keep dropping.

blocks.subTitle: The power wall
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why did clock speeds stop climbing past ~4 GHz?**

Dynamic power grows with frequency, and heat grows with power. Past roughly 4 GHz, cooling a chip cheaply enough to remove that heat stopped being practical — the **power wall**. Higher clocks were technically possible, just not affordable to run.

blocks.subTitle: Why multicore
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why did the industry move to multicore instead of faster single cores?**

The power wall capped single-core clock speed. But Moore's law kept delivering more transistors, so designers used them for extra cores at efficient clocks instead — trading a faster core for more cores, betting software could use them in parallel.

blocks.subTitle: Dynamic vs static power
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Dynamic vs static power — what's the difference?**

**Dynamic power** is burned by transistors switching, roughly proportional to C·V²·f. **Static (leakage) power** is burned by transistors just sitting powered on, current trickling through even when "off." Smaller transistors leak more, so leakage's share keeps growing.

blocks.subTitle: What is DVFS
blocks.markdown:
**Q: What is DVFS and why does it matter?**

Dynamic voltage/frequency scaling lets a chip lower voltage and clock speed when idle-ish, and raise both for demanding bursts. It's how phones and laptops stretch battery life without a fixed slow clock — the chip adapts speed to the moment's need.
